issues.subcategory: retrospective reconstruction mislabeled as prospective/real-time
issues.description: The study retrospectively identifies past suicide attempts and other episodes, then analyzes archived SMS from those windows. This design can examine historical associations with episode labels, but it is not prospective prediction and cannot establish that markers identify risk in real time. Retrospective episode selection is vulnerable to recall bias, dating error, and post hoc selection of salient periods, especially for non-attempt comparison episodes.
issues.quote: By reconstructing the timeline of recent suicidal behaviors through a retrospective clinical interview, we utilized a prospective research design to understand which features in text communications predicted suicide attempt

issues.subcategory: predictive and causal language from retrospective associations
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly frames findings as prediction or real-time identification despite using retrospective within-person comparisons without prospective validation. Associations between language trajectories and retrospectively defined attempts do not demonstrate predictive utility, sensitivity/specificity, clinical accuracy, or causal relevance. This matters because the clinical implication is an imminent-risk monitoring tool, which requires prospective testing against future attempts.
issues.quote: Results suggest private electronic communication has the potential to provide real-time digital markers of suicide risk.

issues.subcategory: non-random episode selection and recall bias
issues.description: Participants retrospectively selected up to three episodes per type and provided dates. The selection of comparison periods may be biased by memory, salience, availability of SMS, or current interpretation. Positive, depressed, and ideation episodes are not objectively sampled from the person's timeline, which undermines within-subject comparability and may induce selection bias.
issues.quote: participants were asked to identify a number of specific events or episodes in the past and the calendar dates during which the episodes took place

issues.subcategory: heterogeneous suicide attempt definition
issues.description: The primary high-risk category combines enacted attempts, interrupted attempts, aborted attempts, and even self-classified incidents without physical action. These states may differ substantially in intent, planning, imminence, lethality, and language patterns. Treating them as one 'suicide attempt episode' weakens construct validity and may obscure or create effects.
issues.quote: past actual, interrupted, or aborted suicide attempts, using the two-week period prior to the attempt as a “suicide attempt episode”

issues.subcategory: self-endorsed attempts not meeting standard attempt definition
issues.description: The manuscript states that some reported 'suicide attempts' involved no enacted physical attempt and were classified based on participants’ subjective endorsement. This is inconsistent with conventional definitions of suicide attempt and creates misclassification between attempt, aborted attempt, planning, and ideation.
issues.quote: reported ‘suicide attempts’ also included incidents in which no physical attempt was enacted but in which participants considered their planning or actions to constitute a higher level of suicidal intent than ‘suicide ideation’ so they subjectively endorsed making an attempt on the screener questions

issues.subcategory: sample size inconsistency for attempters with SMS data
issues.description: The results first state that among 27 participants with SMS data, 15 had data from at least one reported suicide attempt. Shortly afterward, they state that among attempters with SMS data, 13 reported a single lifetime attempt and 14 reported multiple, implying 27 attempters with SMS data. These statements cannot both be true and obscure the actual analytic sample for the main high-risk comparisons.
issues.quote: Among these 27 participants, 15 had data from at least one reported suicide attempt; the other 12 participants contributed data from non-suicide attempt episodes and were still included in the analyses.

issues.subcategory: contradictory attempter counts
issues.description: The statement that 13 participants reported a single lifetime attempt and 14 reported multiple attempts sums to 27 participants, conflicting with the immediately prior statement that only 15 participants had SMS data from at least one attempt. This raises serious uncertainty about which participants contributed attempt episodes and how many independent people inform the key effects.
issues.quote: Among attempters with SMS data, 13 participants reported a single lifetime attempt and 14 reported multiple (M=1.74, SD=0.86).

issues.subcategory: incorrect/misleading likelihood-ratio terminology
issues.description: The manuscript describes likelihood-ratio tests as 'Wald chi-square' tests. Wald tests and likelihood-ratio tests are distinct procedures with different assumptions and statistics. This creates ambiguity about what inferential test was actually used and whether p-values correspond to the reported statistics.
issues.quote: Likelihood-ratio (Wald chi-square) tests were performed to compare goodness of fit for models including and excluding the fixed effect of episode type.

issues.subcategory: incorrect effect-size description for logit coefficients
issues.description: The manuscript states that β values are standardized model parameter estimates in log-odds units. Logit model coefficients are generally unstandardized unless variables were explicitly standardized; no such standardization is described. Calling them standardized effect sizes is misleading and impairs interpretation.
issues.quote: Here, β (standardized values of the model parameter estimates in log odds units) are reported and serve as effect sizes.

issues.subcategory: random intercept for message is not meaningful as specified
issues.description: The proposed random effects include a random intercept for message. Individual SMS messages are observational units and are not repeated across conditions; a message-level random intercept is typically unidentified/redundant with residual error in standard mixed models. If 'message' is a unique ID for every row, including it does not model a meaningful clustering factor and may distort model specification or convergence.
issues.quote: a maximal random effects model, which included random intercepts of participant, episode, and message, and random by-participant slopes

issues.subcategory: unit-of-analysis inflation by message-level modeling
issues.description: The analysis treats 189,478 text messages as model-level observations, but the substantive independent units are participants and episodes, especially only a small number of attempt episodes from few people. Message-level modeling can create an impression of high information while most inferential leverage comes from a small number of persons/episodes; if random effects are inadequate or misspecified, Type I error can be inflated.
issues.quote: This approach also allowed us to maximize sources of variance by analyzing on the message level rather than only mean values by episode

issues.subcategory: binomial denominator and overdispersion not fully reported
issues.description: The LIWC category counts are modeled as proportions of category vs non-category words, which is appropriate in principle, but the manuscript does not report how zero-word messages, very short messages, emojis, non-dictionary tokens, or overdispersion were handled. Text messages are highly variable and sparse; binomial models may underestimate uncertainty if word occurrences within messages are not independent.
issues.quote: These LIWC percentage scores were converted into counts and then entered as proportions in our models (i.e., number of words in a given text message belonging to versus not belonging to the LIWC category)

issues.subcategory: insufficient model specification
issues.description: The manuscript does not provide full formulas, contrast coding, centering/scaling of day, optimizer settings, convergence diagnostics, treatment of singular fits, or exact random-effects structures actually retained for each outcome. This prevents replication and evaluation of the validity of mixed-model inference.
issues.quote: Models were fitted using the “lme4” package in R

issues.subcategory: model simplification after nonconvergence incompletely justified
issues.description: The confirmatory rationale emphasizes maximal random effects, but the slope models did not converge and were reduced to only a by-participant episode-type slope. The choice of this reduced structure, rather than alternatives such as by-participant day slopes, by-episode slopes, Bayesian estimation, or preregistered simplification rules, is not justified and may affect p-values for the key interaction effects.
issues.quote: Models with the full set of random slopes did not converge; therefore, only a by-participant slope of episode type was included in the final model.

issues.subcategory: multiple testing without correction despite many outcomes and contrasts
issues.description: The study tests many LIWC outcomes, two analytic families, omnibus tests, pairwise contrasts, and additional robustness analyses. Several key p-values are borderline (e.g., p=.049, .046), and no multiplicity correction or false discovery control is applied. This substantially increases the probability that the reported 'unique' markers are false positives.
issues.quote: Given this is a pilot study with a small and already potentially underpowered sample and the fact that we did not have concrete directional hypotheses for many of the tests, we decided not to artificially suppress Type I error (i.e., using a multiple comparisons correction)

issues.subcategory: unclear preregistration and exploratory-confirmatory boundary
issues.description: The manuscript says variables were selected a priori but also acknowledges numerous exploratory aspects and uses visual inspection to choose/check the time window. It does not state whether hypotheses, outcomes, preprocessing, model structures, exclusions, or correction plans were preregistered. This leaves substantial researcher degrees of freedom.
issues.quote: Numerous aspects of this research were exploratory by nature.

issues.subcategory: data-informed time-window selection
issues.description: The two-week window is justified theoretically, but the manuscript also reports using visual inspection of 30-day plots to assess the optimal window and notes changes around 7 days. Looking at outcome trajectories to choose or validate the analysis window can capitalize on chance unless clearly separated from confirmatory testing.
issues.quote: The question of the optimal time window was also assessed empirically, using visual inspection of descriptive figures to identify when the rate of change appeared to be most pronounced.

issues.subcategory: power analysis poorly matched to mixed-model design
issues.description: The power analysis references Cramer's V for chi-square tests of mixed-effects models and assumes large effects from between-subject LIWC studies. It is unclear how clustering, number of participants, number of episodes, within-person correlations, random effects, sparse word counts, and unequal episode availability were incorporated. The resulting power claim is not interpretable for the actual GLMM/LMM analyses.
issues.quote: a sample size of 30 suicide attempters (representing 60 attempts but only 20 with collected, usable SMS data, divided by the design effect) would provide enough power to detect only large effect sizes (Cramer’s V=0.29) for chi-square tests of mixed-effects models

issues.subcategory: large missing SMS data by episode
issues.description: Only 134 of 293 identified episodes contained SMS data, meaning more than half of episodes were unavailable for analysis. Missingness is likely nonrandom because it depends on phone type, encryption, age of episode, device changes, backups, and participant behavior. Mixed models do not automatically solve nonrandom missing data, and the manuscript does not analyze predictors of missingness or sensitivity to missing episodes.
issues.quote: Among the episodes queried during the lab interview, 134 (46%) episodes contained SMS data

issues.subcategory: participant-level missingness for core outcome
issues.description: Only 27 of 33 participants contributed any SMS episode data, and apparently only a subset contributed attempt SMS data. Excluding or partially including participants based on data availability can bias results if SMS retention or phone access is associated with age, recency, severity, socioeconomic status, or risk state.
issues.quote: 134 (46%) episodes contained SMS data, collected from 27 different participants

issues.subcategory: missing data incorrectly minimized by mixed-model rationale
issues.description: The manuscript implies mixed models handle the study's missing data, but mixed models generally rely on assumptions such as missing at random conditional on modeled variables. The missing SMS data here likely arise from device/software constraints and episode timing, and no missingness model or sensitivity analysis is reported.
issues.quote: especially appropriate for this dataset given the amount of ‘missing data’ (i.e., participants varied widely in terms of the number of episodes types they reported and for which they had text data)

issues.subcategory: comparison episodes not temporally anchored equivalently
issues.description: Attempt episodes are anchored to a discrete terminal event at day 0, whereas ideation, depressed, and positive episodes are arbitrary two-week periods with no comparable endpoint. Thus slope differences may reflect anchoring artifacts rather than suicide-specific escalation. For comparison episodes, there is 'no theoretical expectation of temporal change,' making the interaction partly a test of event-anchored vs non-event-anchored intervals.
issues.quote: the two weeks leading up to a suicide attempt compared to changes during other two-week periods for episode types of lower suicide risk (for which there is no theoretical expectation of temporal change)

issues.subcategory: social engagement operationalization too crude
issues.description: The interpersonal theory constructs thwarted belongingness and perceived burdensomeness are not adequately captured by aggregate sent/received ratios or message counts. These metrics cannot distinguish supportive vs conflictual exchanges, unanswered outreach, rejection, burdensomeness, or relationship quality, weakening tests of the theory.
issues.quote: decreased social engagement (i.e., lower ratio of sent vs. received text messages)

issues.subcategory: self-focus measured only by first-person singular pronouns
issues.description: First-person singular pronoun use is an imperfect proxy for self-focus and can vary with conversational context, relationship to recipient, syntax, or SMS style. Without validation in this SMS context, interpreting LIWC pronoun frequency as self-focus is tenuous.
issues.quote: we tested whether use of first-person pronouns (as an indicator of self-focus) was greater prior to suicide attempts

issues.subcategory: sentiment constructs inadequately captured by LIWC single-word categories
issues.description: LIWC single-word categories do not capture negation, sarcasm, context, slang, emojis, or conversational meaning. This is especially important for short SMS messages, where context and nonstandard language are common. The manuscript acknowledges this later but still interprets LIWC categories as psychological sentiment markers.
issues.quote: LIWC searches a text file and calculates normalized word counts for nearly 6,400 words, word stems, and emoticons that have been previously categorized into a number of linguistic and psychological dimensions.

issues.subcategory: unclear handling of incoming versus outgoing message content
issues.description: The manuscript analyzes private SMS but does not clearly state whether LIWC language outcomes were computed on outgoing messages only, incoming messages only, or both. If both are included, the language may reflect communication partners rather than the participant's psychological state. This is a critical replicability and construct-validity issue.
issues.quote: Language analysis software scored 189,478 text messages to capture three psychological constructs: self-focus, sentiment, and social engagement.

issues.subcategory: incoming messages may not measure participant state
issues.description: If incoming texts were included in language analyses, they represent other people's word use, not necessarily participants' mental state. Even if incoming texts reflect social context, interpreting them as the attempter's self-focus or sentiment is invalid without explicit modeling by sender direction.
issues.quote: all available SMS data from each device were downloaded (i.e., not from only certain dates or recipients)

issues.subcategory: no descriptive counts by episode type and participant for key analyses
issues.description: The manuscript reports total episodes and total messages but not the number of participants, episodes, messages, and words by episode type used in each model. Without this, readers cannot assess imbalance, sparsity, or whether key findings are driven by one or two participants or episodes.
issues.quote: Across all episodes, 189,478 text messages were collected and analyzed, ranging between on average about 1,200-1,600 text messages per episode.

issues.subcategory: small number of attempt episodes
issues.description: The key claims concern language preceding suicide attempts, but only a small number of attempt episodes with SMS data are reported. Such sparse high-risk data make estimates unstable and highly sensitive to influential participants or episodes.
issues.quote: Among the 21 attempts with corresponding SMS data

issues.subcategory: narrow young college-heavy sample
issues.description: The sample is predominantly young, female, White, and college-aged, recruited partly from a psychology participant pool and one local community. SMS habits and suicide-risk processes may differ by age, sex, culture, clinical severity, socioeconomic status, and technology platform. Generalization to broader suicidal populations is limited.
issues.quote: Most of the participants were female, White, and college-aged.

issues.subcategory: nonfatal and low-lethality events limit application to suicide deaths
issues.description: The study cannot directly generalize to suicide deaths or more medically serious attempts. Most attempt episodes with SMS data involved no physical harm, and the sample excluded people with high current risk. This limits claims about preventing suicide mortality or identifying those at imminent lethal risk.
issues.quote: 71% of incidents did not result in any physical harm

issues.subcategory: exclusion of currently high-risk individuals
issues.description: Participants with intense current suicidal thoughts, plans, or intent were excluded. While ethically understandable, this excludes the population most relevant to imminent-risk detection and may restrict variability in acute-risk language patterns.
issues.quote: Any participants with intense thoughts of suicide who were determined to be at “high risk” or “imminent risk” for suicidal behavior... were excluded from study participation and referred for clinical care.

issues.subcategory: discussion reports anxiety mean effect not present in results
issues.description: The discussion says the high-risk period was associated with greater anxiety and sadness, but the results and Table 2 report no significant episode-type effect for anxiety. This overstates findings and conflicts with the reported statistics.
issues.quote: results indicated that the period of high risk just before a suicide attempt was associated with messages indicating greater anxiety and sadness

issues.subcategory: iatrogenic change sign inconsistency
issues.description: The results state desire to die decreased from pre to post, but Table 1 lists the change as positive 0.20. Depending on the direction of subtraction, this may be a sign error or unclear reporting, and it undermines confidence in descriptive reporting.
issues.quote: desire to die from pre (M=0.82, SD=1.10) to post (M=0.61, SD=0.90) significantly decreased slightly, t(32)=2.23, p=.033.

issues.subcategory: unclear paired t-test direction and clinical significance for iatrogenic assessment
issues.description: The paired t-test for desire to die is statistically significant but extremely small in magnitude and based on a low baseline mean. The manuscript does not clarify direction coding or whether assumptions were met for bounded ordinal 0-10 ratings. Statistical significance here should not be overinterpreted.

issues.subcategory: borderline p-values interpreted as unique markers
issues.description: Key claims that anger increased and positive emotion decreased uniquely before attempts rely partly on pairwise comparisons with p=.049 and p=.046. Given multiple testing, small sample, model simplification, and no correction, these borderline results are fragile.
issues.quote: positive emotion decreased more steeply during attempt episodes compared to all other episode types, including ideation (z=1.96, p=.049)

issues.subcategory: incomplete reporting of confidence intervals and effect magnitudes
issues.description: The tables provide coefficients and standard errors only for significant follow-ups, without confidence intervals, predicted probabilities, odds ratios, or interpretable changes over time. This prevents evaluation of practical or clinical significance, especially for rare LIWC categories like anger and death words.
issues.quote: See Table 3 for full results.

issues.subcategory: missing preprocessing details for SMS text
issues.description: The manuscript does not fully describe how duplicates, group messages, multimedia messages, emojis, autocorrect artifacts, non-English texts, empty messages, timestamps/time zones, sent vs received direction, and message segmentation were handled. These details are essential for replicating SMS language analysis.
issues.quote: participants’ SMS data files were individually cleaned using Python to standardize the encoding of messages and naming of variables across all participants

issues.subcategory: software extraction heterogeneity not evaluated
issues.description: SMS extraction used multiple third-party tools across operating systems. The manuscript does not report validation that tools extracted equivalent fields, complete histories, deleted messages, timestamps, or message directions. Differential extraction failure could bias episode coverage and language counts.
issues.quote: participants with iPhones were instructed to download their SMS text messages using software programs called iExplorer, SynciOS Manager, and SynciOS Data Recovery, and those with Android devices... SMS Backup & Restore and SMS to Text

issues.subcategory: device encryption creates systematic missingness
issues.description: A number of iPhone users could not provide text data due to encryption settings. This missingness may relate to device type, socioeconomic status, privacy behavior, recency, or technical sophistication and could affect representativeness. No comparison of included vs excluded participants is reported.
issues.quote: a number of iPhone users had encryption settings on their phones that prevented third-party iPhone software from accessing text data

issues.subcategory: no blinding of interviewer to study hypotheses
issues.description: The same experimenter collected episode dates and descriptions. There is no report that interviewers were blinded to hypotheses or used standardized structured procedures for anchoring dates across episode types. Interviewer prompts could influence episode selection, classification, and dating.
issues.quote: participants were interviewed by the experimenter and asked to identify a number of episodes

issues.subcategory: unclear reliability of episode classification
issues.description: Episode labels are central to the study, but no interrater reliability, independent clinical coding, or adjudication procedure is reported. The manuscript notes additional questions were asked but does not describe classification rules or thresholds.
issues.quote: Participants answered additional questions about each reported episode as a way to minimize the risk of misclassification

issues.subcategory: overlapping or temporally adjacent episodes not addressed
issues.description: Participants could report multiple episodes of different types. The manuscript does not state whether episode windows could overlap, how overlapping SMS messages were assigned, or how proximity between ideation/depression and attempts was handled. Overlap would violate episode independence and contaminate comparisons.
issues.quote: A total of 3 to 12 episodes were collected for each participant depending on the presence and number of reported events.

issues.subcategory: uncontrolled time-varying confounds
issues.description: Language changes before attempts may be driven by relationship conflict, substance use, exams, hospitalization, medication changes, sleep disruption, or other life events that also influence suicide risk. The within-person design controls stable traits but not time-varying confounders, and these are not modeled.
issues.quote: participants were then asked to describe specific details of and context surrounding each time period

issues.subcategory: lack of control for communication partner/context
issues.description: SMS language depends strongly on who the participant is texting, relationship context, and conversation topic. The analysis removed recipient identifiers and apparently does not model recipient or conversation threads, so differences could reflect texting different people rather than changes in participant state.
issues.quote: identifying information (e.g., message content, sender/recipient names) were removed prior to analysis

issues.subcategory: positive mood comparison may not represent minimal/no suicide risk
issues.description: Positive mood episodes are assumed minimal/no risk, but participants are all suicide attempters and may have fluctuating symptoms. The manuscript relies on retrospective denial of ideation/attempt during selected windows; without contemporaneous assessment, risk classification may be inaccurate.
issues.quote: positive mood (i.e., more positive mood than usual and no ideation or attempt)

issues.subcategory: depressed mood and high stress combined
issues.description: The depressed comparison category includes depressed mood or high stress, which are conceptually and clinically distinct and may have different language signatures. Combining them reduces interpretability of comparisons and may obscure risk gradients.
issues.quote: two-week episodes of depressed mood or high stress (not resulting in suicide ideation or attempt)

issues.subcategory: linear risk hierarchy assumed without validation
issues.description: The study treats attempt, ideation, depressed, and positive episodes as descending levels of suicide risk. However, attempt status is not simply a monotonic severity marker, and depressed/high-stress or positive periods in attempters may not map cleanly onto minimal risk. This hierarchy underlies hypotheses and interpretation but is not independently validated.
issues.quote: attempt episodes were considered “high risk,” ideation episodes were considered “moderate risk,” and depressed and positive episodes were considered “minimal/no risk.”

issues.subcategory: continuous bounded LIWC Tone modeled without distribution details
issues.description: The proprietary LIWC Tone score is bounded and non-transparent, but the manuscript appears to model it using LMM as a raw continuous outcome. Distributional assumptions, transformations, and residual diagnostics are not reported. Bounded skewed outcomes may violate LMM assumptions.
issues.quote: Other LIWC variables include counts of words... and several proprietary, “non-transparent” variables (e.g., Tone)

issues.subcategory: table notation errors obscure chi-square statistics
issues.description: Tables omit the chi-square symbol and contain duplicated df columns and inconsistent headers. This makes statistical reporting unclear and suggests possible formatting or reporting errors in the analysis of deviance tables.

issues.subcategory: p-value typo
issues.description: The p-value for one anger comparison is reported as .0111, inconsistent with the surrounding three-decimal format and likely a typographical error. Minor, but it reflects imprecise reporting.
issues.quote: positive (z=2.54, p=.0111) episodes

issues.subcategory: SMS-only data stream may not capture communication ecology
issues.description: The study collected SMS but many young adults communicate via platforms such as Snapchat, Instagram, WhatsApp, iMessage features, Facebook Messenger, or other apps. Missing communication channels can bias language estimates and limit generalizability of SMS markers to actual digital communication behavior.
issues.quote: Additional forms of personal digital data... were collected for the purposes of future analyses but are not part of the current study.

issues.subcategory: availability of historical SMS linked to recency
issues.description: Participants needed access to messaging data before past attempts. Older attempts, device changes, and platform changes likely reduce data availability, potentially selecting for recent, less severe, or technologically accessible events. This threatens representativeness of attempt episodes.
issues.quote: availability of and access to personal messaging data dating back prior to significant life events (e.g., suicide attempt)

issues.subcategory: episode timing recency not reported
issues.description: The manuscript does not report how long before study participation the episodes occurred, by episode type. Recency affects recall accuracy, SMS availability, technology platform, and participant life stage. Without this information, the reliability of retrospective dating and data completeness cannot be assessed.
issues.quote: Participants were generally confident about the accuracy of the dates they selected

issues.subcategory: confidence in dates insufficient for day-level slope analysis
issues.description: The key slope analysis depends on accurate day-by-day alignment before attempts. Yet 'somewhat certain' dates may be off by a few days, which is large relative to a 14-day window and can distort estimated temporal trajectories.
issues.quote: 90.3% of episodes as ‘very certain’ (i.e., exact days) or ‘somewhat certain’ (i.e., may be off by a few days)

issues.subcategory: day variable coding and interpretation unclear
issues.description: Day is coded from -14 to 0, but models and figures interpret increases 'as one approached an attempt.' Without clear centering, reference day, and sign conventions, coefficients in Table 3 are difficult to interpret and appear counterintuitive in places. The manuscript does not explain how the sign of interaction coefficients maps to plotted slopes.
issues.quote: day of episode (numerical factor ranging from -14 to 0)

issues.subcategory: sparse rare-word outcomes
issues.description: Categories like death, anger, sadness, and anxiety are rare in SMS. The manuscript does not report counts or zero-inflation. Sparse binomial outcomes can yield unstable estimates and convergence issues, especially with complex random effects and small numbers of participants.
issues.quote: No significant effects by episode type emerged for... anxiety, anger, death

issues.subcategory: clinical monitoring claims not supported by accuracy metrics
issues.description: The manuscript discusses notifying clinicians/family based on communication patterns, but the study does not estimate classification accuracy, calibration, positive predictive value, false positive/negative rates, or prospective utility. Clinical implementation claims are premature.
issues.quote: development of an objective monitoring tool capable of tracking individuals’ communication “behind the scenes,” notifying suicidal individuals and/or their clinician or family if their patterns of communication indicate increasing levels of suicide risk

issues.subcategory: overclaim of first study for any clinical outcome
issues.description: The manuscript claims to be the first study to analyze private text messaging data for suicide or any other clinical outcome. This broad novelty claim is difficult to substantiate and not methodologically central, but overclaiming can mislead readers about the evidence base.
issues.quote: This was also the first study, to our knowledge, to collect and analyze private text messaging data for suicide (or any other clinical outcome).

issues.subcategory: misapplication of digital biomarker terminology
issues.description: The study identifies retrospective linguistic associations, not validated biomarkers. A biomarker typically implies reliable, validated measurement with known diagnostic/prognostic properties. Calling LIWC text features 'digital biomarkers' overstates construct maturity.
issues.quote: possible novel, real-time digital biomarkers of suicidal behaviors

issues.subcategory: supplement dependence for essential information
issues.description: Key information needed to evaluate sampling flow, episode descriptives, LIWC variable definitions, model details, and robustness analyses is relegated to supplements not included in the main text. Essential methodological details should be sufficiently summarized for independent evaluation.
issues.quote: See Figure S1 (in the Supplemental Material available online) for a CONSORT diagram detailing specific numbers and reasons for exclusion.

issues.subcategory: CONSORT terminology inappropriate for observational pilot
issues.description: The study is not a randomized trial, so referring to a CONSORT diagram is conceptually imprecise. A STROBE-style flow diagram would be more appropriate. This is minor but reflects some imprecision in methodological framing.
issues.quote: See Figure S1... for a CONSORT diagram detailing specific numbers and reasons for exclusion.

issues.subcategory: no information on language eligibility
issues.description: LIWC English dictionaries require English-language text for valid scoring. The manuscript does not report whether non-English messages or bilingual participants/texts were present and how they were handled.
issues.quote: LIWC searches a text file and calculates normalized word counts

issues.subcategory: no external validation sample
issues.description: Findings are derived and interpreted within the same small pilot sample. Without holdout, replication, or prospective validation, the identified markers may be sample-specific and should not be presented as reliable risk indicators.
issues.quote: This laboratory investigation identified novel predictors of suicidal behaviors

issues.subcategory: pairwise comparisons after significant omnibus inconsistently applied/interpreted
issues.description: For death words, the omnibus interaction is significant but none of the attempt-vs-other pairwise comparisons is significant. The text appropriately notes this, but still includes death among variables whose use changed over time differently as a function of episode type, which may invite overinterpretation unrelated to attempt risk.
issues.quote: There was also a significant interaction for death words... However, there were no significant differences in change over time for attempt compared to all other episodes

issues.subcategory: possible contamination by post-attempt messages on day 0
issues.description: The window is described as -14 to 0 and as the two weeks prior to the attempt. It is unclear whether day 0 includes messages before the attempt only or all messages on the calendar day of the attempt, including after the attempt or after disclosure/intervention. Including post-attempt texts could contaminate predictors with consequences of the attempt.
issues.quote: day of episode (numerical factor ranging from -14 to 0)

issues.subcategory: no handling of time of attempt within day
issues.description: For day-level analysis, an attempt may occur at any time on day 0. The manuscript does not report time-of-day data or exclusion of post-event messages. This is essential for claims about pre-attempt markers.
issues.quote: dates of past suicide attempts... and two-week episodes

issues.subcategory: LIWC word percentages converted from per-message percentages may be lossy
issues.description: The authors convert LIWC percentage scores back into counts. If LIWC outputs rounded percentages or handles stems/emoticons/nonwords in proprietary ways, reconstructing counts from percentages may introduce error. Direct dictionary counts would be more transparent.
issues.quote: These LIWC percentage scores were converted into counts

issues.subcategory: lack of adjustment for total texting volume in language models
issues.description: Although binomial denominators account for word counts within messages, episode-level variation in number of messages and days with no messages may influence estimates. The manuscript does not clarify whether days with no texts are represented in slope analyses for language categories, potentially biasing trajectories toward days with more communication.
issues.quote: Each individual SMS message was inputted into and scored

issues.subcategory: days nested within episodes not modeled explicitly
issues.description: The slope hypotheses concern day-to-day change, but analyses appear to use message-level observations with day as a predictor rather than aggregating or explicitly modeling day-level random effects. Multiple messages on the same day are not independent and days with more messages dominate the slope estimates unless day-level clustering/weights are handled.
issues.quote: A series of mixed-effects models were performed for each language feature with 3 fixed effects: episode type... day of episode... and the interaction

issues.subcategory: potential pseudoreplication from multiple messages per day
issues.description: If each message is a row and no random intercept for day-within-episode is included, many messages on a single high-volume day can disproportionately determine the estimated temporal trend. This is a form of pseudoreplication for daily slope inference.
issues.quote: analyzing on the message level rather than only mean values by episode

issues.subcategory: no influence diagnostics
issues.description: With few participants and attempt episodes, single participants or episodes could drive significant interactions. The manuscript does not report leave-one-participant-out analyses, influence diagnostics, or robustness of key findings to high-volume texters.
issues.quote: Participants reported and had SMS data for on average approximately 1.5 episodes for each episode type.

issues.subcategory: phone ownership and data availability may bias socioeconomic representation
issues.description: Eligibility required access to personal messaging data and devices/backups. This may exclude lower-income individuals, people with unstable housing, lost phones, or less consistent phone access, who may differ in suicide risk and communication patterns.
issues.quote: availability of and access to personal messaging data dating back prior to significant life events

issues.subcategory: escape theory prediction oversimplified
issues.description: The prediction that first-person pronouns should increase before attempts is a narrow operationalization of Baumeister's escape theory. Escape theory involves aversive self-awareness and cognitive deconstruction, not simply self-reference. The theoretical link between pronoun frequency and acute escape motivation is underdeveloped.
issues.quote: It follows that the feedback loop of increasing self-focus and painful recognition of self-failures may lead someone to act on their suicidal thoughts as a means of escape.

issues.subcategory: interpersonal theory constructs conflated with social support volume
issues.description: The interpersonal theory emphasizes perceived burdensomeness and thwarted belongingness, not merely fewer outgoing than incoming messages. The manuscript conflates perceived interpersonal states with communication quantity, making the hypothesis a weak test of the theory.
issues.quote: In theory, social support should combat such feelings and increase feelings of connectedness.

issues.subcategory: unclear exclusion of automated/service texts
issues.description: SMS archives often include automated reminders, two-factor authentication codes, spam, and service messages. The manuscript does not report whether these were removed. Such messages could affect word counts, sentiment, incoming/outgoing ratios, and daily volume.
issues.quote: all available SMS data from each device were downloaded (i.e., not from only certain dates or recipients)

issues.subcategory: no correction for unequal participant contribution
issues.description: Participants varied widely in number of episodes and messages. Although random effects help, high-volume participants may still have disproportionate influence, particularly for fixed effects in message-level models. The manuscript does not report weighting or sensitivity analyses balancing participants or episodes.
issues.quote: ranging between on average about 1,200-1,600 text messages per episode

issues.subcategory: abstract says no mean features differentiated attempts, results show sadness attempt vs ideation
issues.description: The abstract states no language features uniquely differentiated suicide attempts from other episodes. This is technically consistent with lack of uniqueness across all comparisons, but it can obscure the reported significant sad-word mean difference between attempt and ideation. Clearer wording is needed to avoid appearing inconsistent.
issues.quote: Regarding mean differences, no language features uniquely differentiated suicide attempts from other episodes.

issues.subcategory: no contemporaneous clinical state measurement
issues.description: The study infers episode affective and suicidal states retrospectively. There were no ecological momentary assessments or clinical ratings during the SMS windows to validate that the language features correspond to actual momentary risk states.
issues.quote: Participants answered additional questions about each reported episode

issues.subcategory: within-subject design does not eliminate confounding
issues.description: The manuscript implies within-subject comparisons move away from between-subject confounds, but time-varying confounds and differential context remain. Within-person design improves control of stable individual differences but is not sufficient for causal inference about suicide risk processes.
issues.quote: This approach helps avoid the complications inherent to either patient or clinician self-report and moves away from traditional between-subjects comparisons

issues.subcategory: unclear handling of group chats and multiple recipients
issues.description: Group texts can duplicate messages, include multiple conversational partners, and alter sender/recipient dynamics. No details are given on identifying or modeling group chats, which is relevant to social engagement and language context.
issues.quote: SMS text message data from iPhone and Android phones were accessed using third-party software or phone applications.

issues.subcategory: excluded lethal suicide completers by design
issues.description: The study’s motivating problem includes suicide death, but the design necessarily excludes people who died by suicide. The limitation is acknowledged, but conclusions about preventing future suicide-related behaviors should remain constrained to nonfatal attempt-like states in similar young adults.
issues.quote: logistics of accessing and downloading communication data necessitated enrolling participants with non-lethal attempts

issues.subcategory: unclear degrees of freedom for LMM t-tests
issues.description: For LMM outcomes, t statistics and p-values are reported, but lme4 does not provide denominator degrees of freedom or p-values by default. The manuscript does not specify whether Satterthwaite, Kenward-Roger, normal approximation, or another method was used.
issues.quote: pairwise comparisons between each of the episode types (using z and t statistics for binary/proportion and continuous outcome variables, respectively)

issues.subcategory: no descriptive base rates of LIWC categories
issues.description: The manuscript does not report mean proportions or trajectories numerically by episode type for core LIWC categories. Without base rates, readers cannot judge whether statistically significant changes are meaningful or extremely small.
issues.quote: anger increased and positive emotion decreased to a greater extent as one approached a suicide attempt

issues.subcategory: pilot sample underpowered for null conclusions
issues.description: The manuscript acknowledges low power but still interprets null findings for self-focus and social engagement as lack of evidence for utility. Given small N and sparse attempt data, null results are inconclusive.
issues.quote: Therefore, it should be noted that the study was underpowered to detect small- or medium-sized effects and therefore prone to Type II error.

issues.subcategory: ratio outcomes may be ill-defined with zero denominators
issues.description: Social engagement outcomes include ratios of sent vs received words/messages. The manuscript does not report how days or episodes with zero received or zero sent messages were handled. Ratios can be unstable, skewed, or undefined and may require transformation or alternative modeling.
issues.quote: Ratio sent vs. received messages

issues.subcategory: potential survivorship and participation bias
issues.description: Participants willing to share private SMS in a lab study may differ from other attempters in openness, privacy concerns, severity, trust, and communication style. This limits internal and external validity of observed language patterns.
issues.quote: Participants downloaded their communication data in the lab with the experimenter’s assistance

issues.subcategory: IRB/privacy procedures insufficient for third-party texts
issues.description: The study analyzes incoming messages from non-consenting communication partners or at least collected them. The manuscript mentions IRB approval and deidentification but does not describe consent/waiver rationale for third-party private communications, which is important for ethical replicability.
issues.quote: all available SMS data from each device were downloaded (i.e., not from only certain dates or recipients)

issues.subcategory: claim of objective behavioral approach conflicts with retrospective self-report labels
issues.description: The text describes the study as avoiding self-report complications, yet the key outcome/classification variable depends entirely on retrospective self-report of episodes and dates. SMS content is objective in the sense of archived behavior, but labels are not.
issues.quote: This approach helps avoid the complications inherent to either patient or clinician self-report

issues.subcategory: post hoc pairwise contrasts not fully specified
issues.description: The manuscript does not specify whether pairwise comparisons used estimated marginal means, treatment contrasts from the model, releveling, or multiplicity-adjusted procedures. It also reports only significant-family follow-ups. This limits reproducibility.
issues.quote: Any significant tests were followed up with pairwise comparisons between each of the episode types

issues.subcategory: additional robustness analyses relegated and underspecified
issues.description: The manuscript states additional analyses using alternate data subsets were performed, but the main text gives no rationale, selection criteria, or whether these were planned. Alternate subsets can introduce analytic flexibility and selective emphasis.
issues.quote: Additional analyses were performed to examine the same set of outcome variables but in different ways to examine the robustness of the primary results and to see if the pattern of results changed.

issues.subcategory: no code availability for analysis scripts
issues.description: Study materials are said to be on OSF, but the manuscript does not state that preprocessing and analysis code, model formulas, or deidentified derived data are available. Given complex custom SMS processing, code availability is important for reproducibility.
issues.quote: full screening surveys and other study materials are available on OSF at https://osf.io/9f3v2/

issues.subcategory: construct of imminent risk too broad for two-week window
issues.description: The manuscript frames the target as imminent or real-time risk, but analyzes a 14-day pre-attempt period. Imminence in clinical suicide risk often refers to hours to days, and the study does not establish that two-week linguistic slopes can indicate immediate danger.
issues.quote: two weeks preceding a suicide attempt as a means to capture the period of escalation towards a suicide attempt

issues.subcategory: risk-level labels conflate severity and outcome occurrence
issues.description: Labeling attempts as 'high risk' and ideation without attempt as 'moderate risk' is retrospective outcome-based labeling. During the ideation windows, true imminent risk may have been high but no attempt occurred due to interruption, coping, or chance. This can bias interpretation of markers as risk-specific rather than outcome-specific.
issues.quote: In terms of suicide risk levels, attempt episodes were considered “high risk,” ideation episodes were considered “moderate risk,” and depressed and positive episodes were considered “minimal/no risk.”

issues.subcategory: unclear whether models account for multiple episodes within same type per participant
issues.description: Participants could contribute up to three episodes per type. The manuscript includes participant-episode random intercepts, but does not explain episode ID construction or whether repeated same-type episodes and varying time gaps were modeled. Multiple episodes from one participant may not be exchangeable.
issues.quote: For each episode type, we asked about a maximum of three episodes

issues.subcategory: no demographic comparison of SMS contributors vs noncontributors
issues.description: The manuscript reports overall sample demographics but not whether participants/episodes with usable SMS differed from those without data. This is crucial because only SMS contributors are included in inferential analyses.
issues.quote: Preliminary descriptive analyses... were performed on the sample of participants contributing at least one episode of messaging data.

issues.subcategory: ambiguous handling of non-normal count outcomes
issues.description: For outcomes such as number of outgoing/incoming messages, the manuscript says raw continuous variables were used in LMMs. Counts are nonnegative, often skewed and overdispersed; Poisson/negative-binomial or transformed models may be more appropriate. No diagnostics justify LMMs.
issues.quote: For outcome variables that were not proportion scores (e.g., number of messages sent per day), the raw continuous variable was used in a linear mixed-effects model (LMM)

issues.subcategory: arbitrary maximum of three episodes per type
issues.description: Limiting to a maximum of three episodes per type may select more memorable or severe episodes and discard other potentially informative periods. The selection rule for which three episodes were chosen is not described, creating possible bias.
issues.quote: For each episode type, we asked about a maximum of three episodes

issues.subcategory: attempt severity measures not tied to analyses
issues.description: The manuscript reports intent, lethality, and plan presence but does not use them to stratify, adjust, or test whether findings differ for actual vs aborted/interrupted or higher- vs lower-lethality attempts. Given heterogeneity of attempt episodes, this is an important missing analysis or at least a reporting limitation.
issues.quote: participants reported fairly high intent to kill themselves... subjective judgment of the lethality... was reasonably high

issues.subcategory: language may be consequence of escalating crisis rather than marker
issues.description: Even if language changes occur before attempts, they may reflect crisis events or interpersonal conflict that are proximal causes or consequences of distress, not independent markers of suicide risk. The manuscript does not disentangle these mechanisms.
issues.quote: anger increased and positive emotion decreased to a greater extent during the two weeks prior to suicide attempts

issues.subcategory: technology platform changes over historical episodes
issues.description: Because episodes may span past years in young adults, SMS usage patterns may vary with phone ownership, social app adoption, and developmental stage. The manuscript does not report dates/years of episodes or adjust for calendar time.
issues.quote: access to personal messaging data dating back prior to significant life events

issues.subcategory: laboratory recruitment may exclude severe clinical populations
issues.description: Recruitment from a university participant pool and local community, plus requirement to attend a 2-2.5 hour lab session, likely selects relatively functional individuals and excludes more severe or unstable clinical cases.
issues.quote: recruited from the University of Virginia Psychology Department’s participant pool and from the Charlottesville community

issues.subcategory: screening flow insufficient in main text
issues.description: The manuscript says 2,377 online and 77 phone screens were conducted but does not provide main-text numbers for exclusions, refusals, eligible nonparticipants, or reasons. These are important for assessing selection bias.
issues.quote: 2,377 individuals were screened online and 77 individuals were screened by phone

issues.subcategory: p-values for chi-square tests with boundary/random effects may be approximate
issues.description: Likelihood-ratio tests in GLMMs with complex random effects and small clusters can have anti-conservative or poorly calibrated chi-square approximations. The manuscript does not use parametric bootstrap or small-sample correction, despite only 27 participants and few attempt episodes.
issues.quote: Likelihood-ratio... tests were performed to compare goodness of fit

issues.subcategory: actual/enacted attempt percentage vs broad inclusion confusing
issues.description: The sample is described as all having at least one actual/enacted, interrupted, or aborted attempt, with about 80% actual attempts. The study title and many interpretations refer simply to suicide attempts, which can obscure that a substantial portion of participants/episodes involve non-enacted events.
issues.quote: all participants reported a history of at least one actual/enacted, interrupted, or aborted suicide attempt (about 80% reported making an actual suicide attempt)

issues.subcategory: death word null may be due to privacy/censoring rather than risk absence
issues.description: The interpretation that explicit suicide-specific language may not differ ignores that participants may avoid texting about suicide, delete messages, use euphemisms, or communicate via other channels. The measure may not validly capture explicit suicide communication.
issues.quote: use of death-related words did not significantly differ between episodes, suggesting the need to identify hidden and more subtle signs of risk beyond explicit endorsements of suicide-specific language

issues.subcategory: deleted messages not addressed
issues.description: SMS archives may omit deleted messages, which could be especially likely around crises or sensitive suicidal communications. The manuscript does not report whether deleted messages can be recovered by the extraction tools or how deletion bias was considered.
issues.quote: SMS text message data from iPhone and Android phones were accessed using third-party software or phone applications.

issues.subcategory: no information on current treatment/medication as confounders
issues.description: The manuscript collected treatment and diagnosis information but does not report how treatment status, medication, hospitalization, or therapy around episodes were measured or controlled. These may affect both communication and suicide risk.
issues.quote: Participants also reported on current and past treatment experience (e.g., medications, therapy) and psychiatric diagnoses.

issues.subcategory: retrospective comparison episodes may be affected by mood-congruent memory
issues.description: Participants with suicide histories may recall and date mood/ideation/positive episodes in ways influenced by current mood or narratives about past attempts. This can bias episode classification and timing independent of SMS content.
issues.quote: dates and information regarding episodes relied on retrospective self-report, which may not have been entirely reliable

issues.subcategory: figures unavailable/insufficiently reported
issues.description: Figure 1 is referenced for interpreting slopes, but the provided manuscript does not include visible plotted values or confidence bands. The numerical tables do not provide enough information to reconstruct trajectories.
issues.quote: As shown in Figure 1A, self-focus tended to increase preceding an attempt

issues.subcategory: emotional tone follow-up uses t while omnibus uses chi-square without method detail
issues.description: For Tone, the omnibus interaction is reported as chi-square and follow-ups as t-tests, but the methods do not explain how follow-up p-values were computed for LMM contrasts. This is a reporting gap with statistical implications.
issues.quote: emotional tone, 2(3)=26.81, p<.001... depressed episodes (t=4.27, p<.001)

issues.subcategory: machine learning discussion overextends from non-ML analyses
issues.description: The manuscript uses current results to motivate machine learning prediction, but this study does not build or validate a predictive model. Referring to 'novel predictors' and clinical classifiers risks conflating explanatory association tests with predictive modeling.
issues.quote: The results of the current study could also serve as the basis for building a machine learning model to automate identification of text features associated with suicide risk.

issues.subcategory: no correction for autocorrelation over time
issues.description: Messages and daily language within an episode are temporally autocorrelated. The mixed models described do not include autocorrelation structures, which can underestimate standard errors for slope effects.
issues.quote: examining differences in changes in communication over time

issues.subcategory: no negative-control outcomes or periods
issues.description: Given many potential artifacts in SMS timing and retrospective episode selection, negative-control linguistic variables or randomly sampled neutral periods could help assess whether observed slopes are suicide-specific. None are reported.
issues.quote: We analyzed and compared text messages during episodes within person based on a number of features selected a priori

issues.subcategory: significant desire-to-die decrease may reflect regression/demand effects
issues.description: The iatrogenic analysis lacks a control group and involves repeated measurement before/after participation. Any small decrease cannot be attributed to the study being safe or beneficial; it could reflect regression to the mean, demand characteristics, or relief after completion.
issues.quote: desire to die... significantly decreased slightly

issues.subcategory: SMS language may reflect audience management rather than internal state
issues.description: Participants may alter wording depending on recipient and desired impression, especially around suicide risk when concealing distress. The manuscript criticizes self-report concealment but assumes private SMS is resistant, which may not hold for interpersonal communication.
issues.quote: ecologically valid data that accumulates automatically and is thus resistant to biases common to the research process, such as demand characteristics or efforts at impression management

issues.subcategory: no recipient-level deidentification timing relative to analysis
issues.description: The manuscript says identifying information and message content were removed prior to analysis, but LIWC requires message content. It is unclear who had access to raw content, when deidentification occurred, and whether analyses were reproducible after content removal.
issues.quote: After this information was appended, the individual SMS files were then compiled and identifying information (e.g., message content, sender/recipient names) were removed prior to analysis.

issues.subcategory: message content described as identifying information removed before analysis despite LIWC scoring
issues.description: The methods indicate LIWC scoring was done before content removal, then says message content was removed prior to analysis. If statistical analysis used LIWC scores only, this should be clearer; otherwise the sequence sounds contradictory.
issues.quote: Each individual SMS message was inputted into and scored using... LIWC... After this information was appended... identifying information (e.g., message content, sender/recipient names) were removed prior to analysis.

issues.subcategory: comparison of ideation episodes excludes attempts by definition
issues.description: Ideation episodes are defined as not resulting in an attempt, making them retrospectively selected non-transition episodes. This design compares ideation that did not lead to attempts with pre-attempt periods, but cannot estimate prospective transition risk among ideation states without selection bias.
issues.quote: two-week episodes of suicide ideation (not resulting in a suicide attempt)

issues.subcategory: outcome leakage in episode definitions
issues.description: Because attempt episodes are defined by the subsequent occurrence of an attempt and ideation episodes by the absence of an attempt, the outcome is built into the predictor label. This is acceptable for retrospective contrast but problematic for claims about identifying risk states prospectively.
issues.quote: attempt episodes were considered “high risk,” ideation episodes were considered “moderate risk”

issues.subcategory: unclear whether attempted events had medical verification
issues.description: Attempt characteristics are based on participant descriptions, and no medical record or collateral verification is reported. This limits confidence in attempt classification, lethality, and timing.
issues.quote: Based on participants’ description of the objective lethality of the attempt

issues.subcategory: no sensitivity analysis excluding non-enacted attempts
issues.description: Given the broad attempt category, key analyses should test whether results hold for actual/enacted attempts only. The manuscript does not report such sensitivity analyses in the main text, limiting interpretability of 'suicide attempt' findings.
issues.quote: Relatedly, we used a broad definition of what we considered a “suicide attempt episode,” including not only attempts in which some concrete action was initiated... but also interrupted or aborted attempts

issues.subcategory: sex imbalance limits inference to males
issues.description: The sample is 84.8% female, while suicide death risk and communication patterns often differ by sex/gender. Findings may not generalize to males, who are at higher risk for suicide death.
issues.quote: Sex (% female) | 84.8

issues.subcategory: gender measurement unclear
issues.description: The table reports sex as female percentage, but the methods say gender was collected. It is unclear whether sex assigned at birth, gender identity, or both were assessed, and no information is given on nonbinary/transgender participants. This matters for generalizability and suicide-risk characterization.
issues.quote: Participants provided information about their age, gender, race/ethnicity

issues.subcategory: screening based on hopeless sadness may bias sample
issues.description: Participant-pool recruitment first screened for a period of sadness/hopelessness and willingness to be contacted, which may miss attempters whose attempts were not associated with sadness/hopelessness or who did not endorse contact. This can bias the sample toward depressive presentations.
issues.quote: Have you ever had a period of sadness in the past during which you felt hopeless?

issues.subcategory: no report of compensation/incentives
issues.description: The manuscript does not report participant compensation. Incentives may affect willingness to disclose suicidal history and share private data, and are relevant for ethical evaluation and selection bias.
issues.quote: Participants were invited into the laboratory for one 2- to 2.5-hour session

issues.subcategory: ANOVA analogy may be misleading for unbalanced GLMMs
issues.description: The text equates likelihood-ratio tests in complex unbalanced mixed models to omnibus ANOVA tests. While conceptually similar, the distributional assumptions and interpretation differ, especially with sparse, clustered binary/proportion data.
issues.quote: A significant test is conceptually similar to an omnibus test for a predictor in an ANOVA

issues.subcategory: real-time phrasing conflicts with archived laboratory analysis
issues.description: The title and framing imply text messages can identify suicide risk in real time, but the study does not analyze streaming data, deploy real-time detection, or test timeliness. It retrospectively analyzes archived texts in a lab setting.
issues.quote: Can Text Messages Identify Suicide Risk in Real Time?

issues.subcategory: no operational definition of high stress episodes
issues.description: Depressed mood/high stress episodes are used as a comparison condition, but criteria for high stress, duration, severity, and differentiation from depression are not specified. Replication and interpretation are limited.
issues.quote: two-week episodes of depressed mood or high stress

issues.subcategory: omnibus df duplicated in Table 2
issues.description: Table 2 has two df columns for several sections with identical entries, but Table 3 has one df column. This inconsistency makes it unclear whether numerator/denominator df, model df, or residual df are being reported.
issues.quote: Self-Focus | Test | df | df | p

issues.subcategory: no control group without suicide attempt history
issues.description: The within-subject design is appropriate for acute within-person contrasts, but without a non-attempter control group the study cannot determine whether identified text trajectories are specific to suicide attempters or common before other stressful events in young adults.
issues.quote: A sample of 33 participants with at least one reported past suicide attempt

issues.subcategory: risk markers may not be specific to suicide attempts
issues.description: The observed anger increase and positive emotion decrease might precede many acute negative events, conflicts, or crises. The study's comparison episodes may not include matched stressful events with comparable temporal anchoring, so specificity to suicide attempts is unproven.
issues.quote: anger increased and positive emotion decreased to a greater extent during the two weeks prior to suicide attempts, relative to the other episode types

issues.subcategory: no details on safety/risk assessment instrument
issues.description: The phone screen and lab procedures mention a suicide risk assessment instrument but do not identify it, its scoring, training, or reliability. This limits evaluation of participant safety and exclusion criteria.
issues.quote: as determined by a suicide risk assessment instrument

issues.subcategory: possible demand characteristics in episode reporting
issues.description: Although SMS were archived, participants knew the study concerned suicide and digital communication when identifying episodes. Their choices of dates and episodes may be influenced by expectations about what researchers seek.
issues.quote: The purpose of the phone screen was to provide potential participants with more information about the study

issues.subcategory: no Bayesian or uncertainty emphasis despite pilot sample
issues.description: The manuscript relies on dichotomous p-value thresholds in a small exploratory pilot rather than emphasizing estimation uncertainty. This increases risk of overinterpreting unstable findings.
issues.quote: A significant test is conceptually similar to an omnibus test

issues.subcategory: unclear treatment of MMS and iMessage distinctions
issues.description: The manuscript refers to SMS text messages, but iPhone archives may include iMessages and MMS, while extraction tools differ. It is unclear which message types were included and whether platform differences affected content availability.
issues.quote: SMS text message data from iPhone and Android phones were accessed

issues.subcategory: word-level LIWC ignores conversational sequence
issues.description: The constructs of social engagement and sentiment in interpersonal communication often depend on turn-taking and context. Single-message LIWC scoring ignores conversational sequence and replies, limiting construct validity for dynamic interpersonal risk processes.
issues.quote: Each individual SMS message was inputted into and scored using... LIWC

issues.subcategory: no assessment of whether participants used SMS during episodes
issues.description: Periods with fewer SMS or migration to other apps may reflect communication platform choice rather than social disengagement or sentiment change. The manuscript does not report platform use during historical windows.
issues.quote: Additional forms of personal digital data... were collected... but are not part of the current study.

issues.subcategory: US single-site sample
issues.description: Participants were recruited from one US university/community context. Findings may not generalize internationally or to populations with different texting norms, languages, healthcare systems, or suicide-risk profiles.
issues.quote: recruited from the University of Virginia Psychology Department’s participant pool and from the Charlottesville community

issues.subcategory: possible separation/estimation problems in rare categories not discussed
issues.description: Rare LIWC categories such as death words may have many zero messages, increasing risk of quasi-separation in logistic mixed models. The manuscript does not report convergence warnings, singularity, or estimation diagnostics by outcome.

issues.subcategory: no participant-level random effects estimates reported
issues.description: The claimed benefit of mixed models is accounting for participant, episode, and message variability, but variance components are not reported. Readers cannot evaluate how much variability exists at each level or whether random effects are justified/singular.
issues.quote: Using mixed models allowed us to account for variability among participants, episodes, and messages

issues.subcategory: safety exclusion threshold inconsistent within protocol
issues.description: Phone screening allowed 'minimal or no current desire to die' defined as <=5 and no plan/intent, while lab risk assessment used >3 on desire to hurt self question as elevated. The thresholds and constructs differ, and the rationale is not explained.
issues.quote: minimal or no current desire to die (i.e., less than or equal to 5 on a 0-10 Likert scale and no current suicide plan/intent)

issues.subcategory: desire to die vs desire to hurt self wording inconsistency
issues.description: The risk assessment alternates between desire to die and desire to hurt self, which are not equivalent constructs. This affects interpretation of screening and safety thresholds.
issues.quote: score greater than 3 on desire to hurt self question

issues.subcategory: no clinical diagnostic verification
issues.description: Psychiatric diagnoses and treatment history are self-reported. No structured diagnostic interview results are reported, limiting characterization of the sample and ability to assess clinical confounding.
issues.quote: Participants also reported on current and past treatment experience... and psychiatric diagnoses.

issues.subcategory: claims about objective tools avoiding concealment overstate SMS utility
issues.description: Private messages may also be concealed, deleted, shifted to other platforms, or written strategically. The study does not test whether SMS markers identify risk when self-report is concealed or unavailable.
issues.quote: This approach helps avoid the complications inherent to either patient or clinician self-report

issues.subcategory: no familywise distinction between primary and secondary outcomes
issues.description: The manuscript has multiple constructs and variables but does not clearly designate a single primary endpoint. Without prioritization, interpretation of significant findings among many tests is vulnerable to selective emphasis.
issues.quote: we focused on testing for both mean and slope differences... for the three previously discussed psychological constructs

issues.subcategory: hypotheses directional but tests apparently two-sided and many exploratory
issues.description: The manuscript states directional hypotheses for some variables but not for means versus slopes or comparison patterns. It does not specify whether tests were one- or two-sided, how directional hypotheses affected inference, or which analyses were confirmatory.
issues.quote: we did not have hypotheses on whether language differences would be observed for episodes overall (means) but not changes over time (slopes), or vice versa

issues.subcategory: comparison windows may differ in life stage and context
issues.description: A participant's attempt, ideation, depressed, and positive episodes may occur years apart, across adolescence/college transitions, different relationships, and different phone habits. The models do not appear to adjust for age/time since episode or calendar year.
issues.quote: specific events or episodes in the past and the calendar dates during which the episodes took place

issues.subcategory: no reporting of episode chronological distribution
issues.description: The manuscript does not report whether episode types were balanced in recency or chronological order. If attempts tended to occur earlier or later than positive/depressed periods, language differences could be confounded by developmental or technological changes.
issues.quote: A total of 3 to 12 episodes were collected for each participant

issues.subcategory: unbalanced classes not sufficient justification for generalizability
issues.description: The manuscript claims mixed models produce generalizable population estimates despite a highly selected, small, unbalanced sample. Mixed models can handle unbalanced data under assumptions but cannot overcome sampling bias or sparse clusters.
issues.quote: leading to more accurate and generalizable population estimates for within-subject effects of episode type

issues.subcategory: emotional tone proprietary nontransparent variable
issues.description: The Tone variable is proprietary and non-transparent, making it difficult to evaluate what psychological construct it measures or reproduce results across tools/versions. Interpretation as upbeat/positive language should be cautious.
issues.quote: several proprietary, “non-transparent” variables (e.g., Tone)

issues.subcategory: no LIWC dictionary coverage statistics
issues.description: The manuscript does not report the proportion of words recognized by LIWC, by episode type or overall. Low or differential coverage in SMS slang/emoji-heavy texts would affect validity of LIWC-derived measures.
issues.quote: LIWC searches a text file and calculates normalized word counts

issues.subcategory: limited current-risk range due to exclusion may affect iatrogenic findings
issues.description: The iatrogenic effects analysis is conducted after excluding people at high/imminent current risk, so it cannot generalize to more acutely suicidal participants who might respond differently to assessment.
issues.quote: no participants ended up being at high or imminent risk

issues.subcategory: use of raw Likert means and t-tests for bounded scales
issues.description: Mood and desire-to-die ratings are bounded ordinal 0-10 scales with likely skew, particularly desire to die near zero. Paired t-tests may be acceptable descriptively but assumptions and robustness are not discussed.
issues.quote: 0 to 10 negative mood and desire to die rating scales

issues.subcategory: mood change direction table unclear
issues.description: Table 1 lists 'Mood (0-10) | -0.20' while text says mood decreased from 6.33 to 6.12, consistent if post-pre. But desire to die decreased from 0.82 to 0.61 while table lists +0.20, inconsistent with the same direction.
issues.quote: Iatrogenic – change pre to post | Mood (0-10) | -0.20 | Desire to die (0-10) | 0.20

issues.subcategory: historical SMS from smartphone users only
issues.description: Eligibility required smartphone/message archive access, which excludes people without smartphones or with limited digital footprints. This limits applicability of digital phenotyping tools to populations with reliable device access.
issues.quote: Participants downloaded their communication data in the lab

issues.subcategory: no detailed inclusion/exclusion criteria for SMS usability
issues.description: The manuscript does not specify what constituted usable SMS data, minimum number of messages/words per episode, or whether episodes with very sparse texts were excluded. Sparse episodes could bias estimates or create unstable slopes.
issues.quote: 134 (46%) episodes contained SMS data

issues.subcategory: day-level zero communication ignored for language proportions
issues.description: If no messages occurred on a given day, that day provides information about social withdrawal but no LIWC language proportion. The model of message-level language excludes silent days, so language slopes are conditional on texting and not on overall communication behavior.
issues.quote: Each individual SMS message was inputted into and scored

issues.subcategory: sent/received ratios separated from language content but not integrated
issues.description: The study analyzes language and social engagement separately, but changes in who texts whom and how often may confound language category proportions. For example, more incoming crisis-support messages could alter observed positive emotion or anger if incoming texts are included.
issues.quote: social engagement (i.e., daily word/message counts for, and ratio between, outgoing and incoming messages)

issues.subcategory: no exact wording for episode interview prompts
issues.description: The manuscript does not provide in the main text the exact interview questions used to elicit episode dates and classify episode types. Because labels are central, exact prompts are needed to assess measurement validity.
issues.quote: Participants were then asked to describe specific details of and context surrounding each time period.

issues.subcategory: slope linearity assumed over 14 days
issues.description: The models assume linear change over day from -14 to 0. The methods note visual patterns were variable and often around 7 days, suggesting nonlinear changes. A linear slope may misrepresent trajectories and affect interaction tests.
issues.quote: day of episode (numerical factor ranging from -14 to 0)

issues.subcategory: visual inspection suggests alternative 7-day window but main 14-day choice retained
issues.description: The authors looked at 30-day loess plots and observed changes around 7 days. This could motivate multiple possible windows or nonlinear specifications. Without preregistered window selection, there is risk of undisclosed analytic flexibility.
issues.quote: changes tended to occur most notably and often around 7 days prior to the suicide attempt

issues.subcategory: lower-risk periods may include acute nonsuicidal crises
issues.description: Depressed/high stress and ideation periods may vary in acute crisis level. Without matching on stressors, observed differences may reflect crisis specificity rather than suicide specificity.
issues.quote: depressed mood or high stress (not resulting in suicide ideation or attempt)

issues.subcategory: lack of cluster-robust sensitivity analyses
issues.description: Given possible model misspecification and small clusters, cluster-robust standard errors or participant-level aggregation sensitivity analyses would help assess robustness. None are reported in the main text.
issues.quote: Mixed-effects models tested whether these constructs differed

issues.subcategory: no data on number of words per message/episode by condition
issues.description: LIWC proportions and binomial precision depend on word counts. The manuscript reports message counts but not word counts by episode type, despite modeling word-category counts.

issues.subcategory: comparison episodes may have been chosen after knowing SMS availability
